subtitle: Step through 10 turning points from post-Roman timber halls, Sutton Hoo, and Lindisfarne (AD 793) to Alfred the Great, Viking Jorvik, Athelstan, Cnut, and 1066.

milestones.title: Angles, Saxons & Jutes Cross the North Sea
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Which pagan Anglo-Saxon gods gave their names to Wednesday and Thursday?
milestones.imageCaption: Reconstructed Anglo-Saxon timber hall and village houses at West Stow in Suffolk.
milestones.provenance: West Stow Country Park / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)
milestones.catalyst: After Roman legions sailed away around AD 410, salty tides flooded coastal farms in Jutland and northern Germany. Families of Angles, Saxons, and Jutes crossed the North Sea in clinker-built rowing ships to farm Britain’s fertile valleys and build thatched timber halls.
milestones.turningPoint: Anglo-Saxon children gathered firewood, spun sheep’s wool on drop-spindles, tended pigs in oak woods, and listened to riddle contests and harp songs in smoky timber halls.
milestones.impact: They formed seven rival kingdoms (Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, and Wessex) and gave us village names ending in -ham and -ton plus Tuesday–Friday!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (AD 597 & 635): Christian Missionaries, Illuminated Gospels & Bede.

ks2.story: After Roman legions sailed away around AD 410, salty tides flooded coastal farms in Jutland and northern Germany. Families of Angles, Saxons, and Jutes crossed the North Sea in clinker-built rowing ships to farm Britain’s fertile valleys and build thatched timber halls.
ks2.significance: They formed seven rival kingdoms (Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, and Wessex) and gave us village names ending in -ham and -ton plus Tuesday–Friday!
ks2.childrenLife: Anglo-Saxon children gathered firewood, spun sheep’s wool on drop-spindles, tended pigs in oak woods, and listened to riddle contests and harp songs in smoky timber halls.
ks2.quote: “Those who came over were of the three most powerful nations of Germany—that is, the Saxons, the Angles, and the Jutes.” — Venerable Bede, AD 731 (tr. Giles 1847)
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Which pagan Anglo-Saxon gods gave their names to Wednesday and Thursday?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Woden (chief god -> Woden’s day / Wednesday) and Thunor (god of thunder -> Thunor’s day / Thursday)!

milestones.title: Christian Missionaries, Illuminated Gospels & Bede
milestones.enquiryQuestion: From which TWO places did Christian missionaries travel to convert Anglo-Saxon kingdoms?
milestones.imageCaption: Hand-painted illuminated page from the Lindisfarne Gospels, created on calfskin vellum using crushed minerals and feather quills.
milestones.catalyst: Christianity reached Anglo-Saxon kingdoms from two directions: Pope Gregory sent monk Augustine to Canterbury in Kent in AD 597, while Irish-Scottish monk Aidan sailed from Iona to found Lindisfarne monastery in Northumbria in AD 635.
milestones.turningPoint: Young boy and girl pupils (such as young Bede at seven years old!) learned to read, sing psalms, mix colorful inks from berries and lapis stone, and write neatly with goose-quill pens.
milestones.impact: Monasteries brought schools, stone churches, Latin and Old English writing on calfskin vellum, and England’s first great historian—the Venerable Bede at Jarrow (AD 731).
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. AD 625): The Royal Ship Burial Inside Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo.

ks2.story: Christianity reached Anglo-Saxon kingdoms from two directions: Pope Gregory sent monk Augustine to Canterbury in Kent in AD 597, while Irish-Scottish monk Aidan sailed from Iona to found Lindisfarne monastery in Northumbria in AD 635.

ks2.childrenLife: Young boy and girl pupils (such as young Bede at seven years old!) learned to read, sing psalms, mix colorful inks from berries and lapis stone, and write neatly with goose-quill pens.
ks2.quote: “Ever since I became a priest, it has been my delight always either to learn, or to teach, or to write.” — Venerable Bede, Ecclesiastical History (AD 731)
ks2.detectiveQuestion: From which TWO places did Christian missionaries travel to convert Anglo-Saxon kingdoms?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: From Rome in the south (Augustine at Canterbury, AD 597) and from Iona in Scotland in the north (Aidan at Lindisfarne, AD 635)!

milestones.title: The Royal Ship Burial Inside Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did archaeologists find NO wooden planks or skeleton inside Sutton Hoo Mound 1?
milestones.imageCaption: The famous Sutton Hoo warrior helmet with gilded dragon eyebrows and stamped bronze warrior panels.
milestones.catalyst: In 1939 in Suffolk, Edith Pretty and archaeologist Basil Brown uncovered the ghostly 27-metre iron-rivet outline of an Anglo-Saxon burial ship—likely built around AD 625 for King Raedwald of East Anglia.
milestones.turningPoint: Children in East Anglia watched teams of oxen haul a 27-metre seagoing ship up the steep river bluff to bury their king with treasures from across the known world.
milestones.impact: Inside lay a dragon-browed helmet, gold-and-garnet clasps with gems from Sri Lanka, Byzantine silver spoons, and Frankish coins—shattering the myth of a backward "Dark Age"!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (AD 793): Dragon Prows Strike Lindisfarne Monastery.

ks2.story: In 1939 in Suffolk, Edith Pretty and archaeologist Basil Brown uncovered the ghostly 27-metre iron-rivet outline of an Anglo-Saxon burial ship—likely built around AD 625 for King Raedwald of East Anglia.
ks2.significance: Inside lay a dragon-browed helmet, gold-and-garnet clasps with gems from Sri Lanka, Byzantine silver spoons, and Frankish coins—shattering the myth of a backward "Dark Age"!
ks2.childrenLife: Children in East Anglia watched teams of oxen haul a 27-metre seagoing ship up the steep river bluff to bury their king with treasures from across the known world.
ks2.quote: “Only rows of rusted iron ship rivets remained in the sand—yet inside the treasure chamber glittered gold and red garnets untouched for 1,300 years.”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why did archaeologists find NO wooden planks or skeleton inside Sutton Hoo Mound 1?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Suffolk’s acidic sandy soil completely rotted away organic wood and human bones over 1,300 years, leaving iron ship rivets and gold treasures behind!

milestones.title: Dragon Prows Strike Lindisfarne Monastery
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Did real Viking raiders wear helmets with horns sticking out of the sides?
milestones.imageCaption: Carved 9th-century gravestone from Lindisfarne showing Viking raiders marching shoulder-to-shoulder brandishing battle-axes and swords.
milestones.catalyst: Without warning on 8 June AD 793, Scandinavian raiders rowed shallow-draught clinker longships directly onto the sandy beach of Holy Island and raided St Cuthbert’s unguarded monastery at Lindisfarne.
milestones.turningPoint: Terrified novice monks hid jewelled manuscripts as shockwaves spread across European courts from Northumbria to Charlemagne’s palace.
milestones.impact: Their clinker-built oak ships drew barely 1 metre of water—letting Vikings cross stormy seas under sail and row straight up shallow rivers before armies could stop them.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (AD 865–874): The Great Heathen Army Conquers Three Kingdoms.

ks2.story: Without warning on 8 June AD 793, Scandinavian raiders rowed shallow-draught clinker longships directly onto the sandy beach of Holy Island and raided St Cuthbert’s unguarded monastery at Lindisfarne.
ks2.significance: Their clinker-built oak ships drew barely 1 metre of water—letting Vikings cross stormy seas under sail and row straight up shallow rivers before armies could stop them.
ks2.childrenLife: Terrified novice monks hid jewelled manuscripts as shockwaves spread across European courts from Northumbria to Charlemagne’s palace.
ks2.quote: “In this year fierce, foreboding omens came over Northumbria... and the ravaging of heathen men miserably destroyed God’s church at Lindisfarne.” — Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, AD 793 (tr. Ingram 1823)
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Did real Viking raiders wear helmets with horns sticking out of the sides?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Never! Real Viking helmets (like Gjermundbu and Coppergate) were smooth iron cones with nose-guards; horned helmets were invented for 19th-century operas.

milestones.title: The Great Heathen Army Conquers Three Kingdoms
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How was the AD 865 Great Heathen Army different from earlier Viking raiders?
milestones.imageCaption: The 9th-century clinker-built Gokstad oak longship, preserved in blue clay and capable of carrying over 60 warriors across open sea.
milestones.provenance: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)
milestones.catalyst: In AD 865, summer hit-and-run raids changed forever when a huge Scandinavian fleet—called the "Great Heathen Army" by monks and led by Ivar the Boneless and Halfdan—landed in East Anglia to stay over winter and conquer farmland.
milestones.turningPoint: Families across Yorkshire and the East Midlands saw Scandinavian warriors hang up their shields, bring families over, and begin ploughing new farms.
milestones.impact: Fortifying winter camps like Repton, the Vikings captured York (AD 866), East Anglia (AD 869), and Mercia (AD 874)—leaving Wessex as the last surviving Anglo-Saxon kingdom!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (AD 878–886): King Alfred Saves Wessex & Agrees the Danelaw.

ks2.story: In AD 865, summer hit-and-run raids changed forever when a huge Scandinavian fleet—called the "Great Heathen Army" by monks and led by Ivar the Boneless and Halfdan—landed in East Anglia to stay over winter and conquer farmland.
ks2.significance: Fortifying winter camps like Repton, the Vikings captured York (AD 866), East Anglia (AD 869), and Mercia (AD 874)—leaving Wessex as the last surviving Anglo-Saxon kingdom!
ks2.childrenLife: Families across Yorkshire and the East Midlands saw Scandinavian warriors hang up their shields, bring families over, and begin ploughing new farms.
ks2.quote: “And the same year came a great heathen army into England, and took up winter quarters among the East Angles, and there were supplied with horses.” — Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, AD 865
ks2.detectiveQuestion: How was the AD 865 Great Heathen Army different from earlier Viking raiders?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Earlier Vikings raided in summer and sailed home; the Great Heathen Army stayed all winter in fortified camps to conquer kingdoms and settle permanently!

milestones.date: May AD 878 • Battle of Edington & Danelaw
milestones.title: King Alfred Saves Wessex & Agrees the Danelaw
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What was the name of the region north and east of Watling Street where Viking laws and "-by" villages flourished?
milestones.imageCaption: The gold, cloisonné-enamel, and rock-crystal Alfred Jewel ("AELFRED MEC HEHT GEWYRCAN" — "Alfred ordered me to be made").
milestones.catalyst: Forced into Somerset’s Athelney marshes after Guthrum’s surprise winter attack in January AD 878, King Alfred rallied the Wessex fyrd and defeated Guthrum at Edington. Guthrum was baptised and agreed a treaty dividing England along Roman Watling Street.
milestones.turningPoint: Noble and freeborn children at Alfred’s court learned to read Old English books before training in hunting or swordsmanship, while villagers lived within 20 miles of a safe walled burh.
milestones.impact: Alfred protected Wessex with 33 walled burhs (like Wareham), built taller ships, translated books into Old English, and launched the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle—earning the title "Alfred the Great".
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. AD 900): Coppergate Craftworkers & Baghdad Silver in Jorvik.

milestones.title: Coppergate Craftworkers & Baghdad Silver in Jorvik
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What does the Viking street name "Coppergate" in York actually mean in Old Norse?
milestones.imageCaption: Silver Islamic dirham coins minted in Central Asia and the Middle East, carried thousands of miles along river routes by Viking merchants.
milestones.catalyst: Beneath Coppergate ("Street of the Cup-Makers") in York—Viking Jorvik—wet peaty soil preserved 40,000 everyday objects: timber workshops, leather boots, antler combs, hnefatafl board games, Byzantine silk, and silver dirham coins from Baghdad!
milestones.turningPoint: Children in Jorvik skated across frozen rivers on polished horse-bone ice skates, spun wooden tops, played strategy board games, and learned leatherwork and wood-turning.
milestones.impact: Coppergate archaeology proved Vikings were neat, skilled craftworkers, farmers, law-makers at outdoor Thing assemblies, and global traders—not just raiders.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (AD 917–937): Aethelflaed & King Athelstan Unite All England.

ks2.story: Beneath Coppergate ("Street of the Cup-Makers") in York—Viking Jorvik—wet peaty soil preserved 40,000 everyday objects: timber workshops, leather boots, antler combs, hnefatafl board games, Byzantine silk, and silver dirham coins from Baghdad!
ks2.significance: Coppergate archaeology proved Vikings were neat, skilled craftworkers, farmers, law-makers at outdoor Thing assemblies, and global traders—not just raiders.
ks2.childrenLife: Children in Jorvik skated across frozen rivers on polished horse-bone ice skates, spun wooden tops, played strategy board games, and learned leatherwork and wood-turning.
ks2.quote: Every time you say sky, window, egg, knife, leg, husband, law, or Thursday, you are speaking Old Norse words left behind by Viking settlers!
ks2.detectiveQuestion: What does the Viking street name "Coppergate" in York actually mean in Old Norse?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: "Street of the Cup-Makers" (from Old Norse koppari = cup-maker and gata = street)!

milestones.title: Aethelflaed & King Athelstan Unite All England
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Who was "Lady of the Mercians", and which grandson of Alfred became the first King of All England in AD 927?
milestones.imageCaption: Illuminated manuscript portrait painted around AD 934 showing crowned King Athelstan presenting a Gospel book to St Cuthbert—the oldest surviving portrait of an English king.
milestones.provenance: Corpus Christi College MS 183 / Public Domain
milestones.catalyst: Alfred’s fearless daughter Aethelflaed ("Lady of the Mercians") built Mercian burhs and recaptured Derby and Leicester. In AD 927 her nephew King Athelstan captured Viking York and defeated northern allies at Brunanburh (AD 937).
milestones.turningPoint: Across newly united shires, silver pennies carried one king’s portrait and royal courts enforced shared laws across Saxon and Anglo-Danish towns alike.
milestones.impact: King Athelstan—not Alfred—became the very first king to rule one united Kingdom of England from the Channel to Northumbria!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (AD 1016–1035): Danegeld & King Cnut’s North Sea Empire.

ks2.story: Alfred’s fearless daughter Aethelflaed ("Lady of the Mercians") built Mercian burhs and recaptured Derby and Leicester. In AD 927 her nephew King Athelstan captured Viking York and defeated northern allies at Brunanburh (AD 937).
ks2.significance: King Athelstan—not Alfred—became the very first king to rule one united Kingdom of England from the Channel to Northumbria!
ks2.childrenLife: Across newly united shires, silver pennies carried one king’s portrait and royal courts enforced shared laws across Saxon and Anglo-Danish towns alike.
ks2.quote: “Athelstan, King of the English and ruler of all Britain.” — Royal charter and coin title after AD 927
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Who was "Lady of the Mercians", and which grandson of Alfred became the first King of All England in AD 927?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Aethelflaed was Lady of the Mercians, and her nephew King Athelstan became the first King of All England!

milestones.title: Danegeld & King Cnut’s North Sea Empire
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did paying silver "Danegeld" bribes fail to stop Viking raids under King Aethelred?
milestones.imageCaption: 1031 New Minster Liber Vitae illumination showing Danish King Cnut and Queen Emma placing a golden cross upon the church altar at Winchester.
milestones.provenance: British Library Stowe MS 944 / Public Domain
milestones.catalyst: When huge Danish fleets returned in the 990s, King Aethelred paid vast sums of silver Danegeld that only tempted raiders back. From AD 1016 to 1035, Danish King Cnut ruled England, Denmark, and Norway together in peace.
milestones.turningPoint: Merchant ships sailed safely between London, York, Denmark, and Norway during nearly twenty years of peace across Cnut’s North Sea Empire.
milestones.impact: Cnut kept Anglo-Saxon laws, married Queen Emma, protected English monasteries, and guarded Britain’s coasts with his own fleet before Edward the Confessor restored Saxon rule.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (Sept–Oct 1066): Stamford Bridge to Hastings — End of an Era.

ks2.story: When huge Danish fleets returned in the 990s, King Aethelred paid vast sums of silver Danegeld that only tempted raiders back. From AD 1016 to 1035, Danish King Cnut ruled England, Denmark, and Norway together in peace.
ks2.significance: Cnut kept Anglo-Saxon laws, married Queen Emma, protected English monasteries, and guarded Britain’s coasts with his own fleet before Edward the Confessor restored Saxon rule.
ks2.childrenLife: Merchant ships sailed safely between London, York, Denmark, and Norway during nearly twenty years of peace across Cnut’s North Sea Empire.
ks2.quote: “I have vowed to God to rule all my kingdoms justly and piously, keeping the laws of King Edgar.” — King Cnut’s Letter to the English People (AD 1027)
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why did paying silver "Danegeld" bribes fail to stop Viking raids under King Aethelred?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Because Viking fleets realised England had rich silver mints and kept coming back demanding even bigger payments!

milestones.title: Stamford Bridge to Hastings — End of an Era
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Which two rival invaders did King Harold Godwinson fight within nineteen days in autumn 1066?
milestones.imageCaption: 11th-century Bayeux Tapestry scene showing King Harold II enthroned with orb and sceptre after Edward the Confessor’s death in January 1066.
milestones.catalyst: When childless Edward the Confessor died in January 1066, newly crowned King Harold Godwinson marched 185 miles north in four days to defeat Viking King Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge (25 Sept)—then marched 250 miles south to face Duke William of Normandy at Hastings (14 Oct).
milestones.turningPoint: Across autumn 1066, families watched Halley’s Comet blaze across the night sky and heard news of two giant battles fought within nineteen dramatic days.
milestones.impact: Stamford Bridge ended the Viking Age in England forever, while nineteen days later William’s victory at Hastings ended Anglo-Saxon royal rule and began Norman England!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Completes all 10 turning points in Anglo-Saxons & Vikings (AD 410–1066).

ks2.childrenLife: Across autumn 1066, families watched Halley’s Comet blaze across the night sky and heard news of two giant battles fought within nineteen dramatic days.
ks2.quote: “HERE SITS HAROLD, KING OF THE ENGLISH (HIC RESIDET HAROLD REX ANGLORUM).” — Latin embroidery on the Bayeux Tapestry

ks2.detectiveAnswer: Norwegian Viking King Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge (25 September) and Duke William of Normandy at Hastings (14 October)!
